query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐deposited Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 high-entropy alloy films and nanoribbons, the magnetocaloric response and associated hysteresis are primarily governed by the extent of localized short-range atomic order and residual internal strain. Relieving this strain by 700 K annealing induces subtle atomic reordering that reduces domain-pinning barriers, thereby enhancing collective ferromagnetic alignment, increasing the effective magnetization and isothermal magnetic entropy change during low-applied-field cycles, while also reducing hysteresis.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, rare-earth-free Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 thin films and lithographically patterned nanoribbon arrays on substrates; the material is amorphous or extremely fine/disordered with a single cubic-type short-range order and a smooth surface.
generation.intervention: Annealing the 1 µm-spaced nanoribbons at 700 K in flowing Ar + 2% N2 at a heating rate of 10 K/min (and/or applying controlled cyclic longitudinal tensile strain up to 2% in the elastic regime) to relieve fabrication-induced internal strain and promote short-range atomic reordering without triggering bulk crystallization.
generation.conditions: Measurements to be performed under identical conditions for both as-deposited and post-annealing samples, using established SQUID magnetometry (including parallel vs. perpendicular M(H) loops and ZFC/FC M(T) curves) over a temperature range (e.g., 40–200 K) relevant to the broad conventional response, with strain maintained within the 0–2% elastic regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range atomic reordering and relaxation of internal, fabrication-induced strain without bulk crystallization mediate changes in domain-pinning barriers and magnetic coupling, preserving the overall amorphous matrix.
generation.mechanism: Annealing relieves internal stresses and induces subtle short-range atomic reordering, which reduces local domain-pinning centers and enhances collective exchange interactions. This results in increased effective ferromagnetic volume and higher magnetization under low-applied fields, leading to an improved conventional isothermal magnetic entropy change and lower hysteresis during magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited 1 µm-spaced nanoribbon baseline (with −ΔSM ≈ 1.25 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 140 K under ΔH = 50 kOe), the 700 K annealing should increase maximum magnetization and the magnitude of the conventional −ΔSM (without introducing bulk crystalline phases) and reduce hysteretic losses. Additionally, applying elastic longitudinal strain is predicted to stabilize the magnetic order (especially above 100 K) without shifting the blocking peak.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, unannealed and unstrained Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 films or 1 µm-spaced nanoribbon arrays measured under identical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the metastable, pre-crystallization regime (annealing at 700 K) and for strain levels confined to the elastic range (up to 2%). It is expected to hold for the broad temperature range (approximately 40–200 K) over which the conventional magnetocaloric response has been observed; deviations may occur near temperatures (e.g., <20 K) where different magnetic phenomena (such as edge-related spin frustration) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise magnitude of the enhancements in magnetocaloric properties and the degree to which strain-induced anisotropies might interplay with annealing effects. Variability in processing conditions could also influence the threshold for bulk crystallization versus beneficial short-range reordering.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of 1 µm-spaced nanoribbon arrays from the same as-deposited batch. Subject one set to 700 K annealing under the specified conditions while keeping the other set as a control. Characterize both sets using TEM/SAED and AFM to confirm the absence of bulk crystallization along with subtle signs of short-range atomic reordering and strain relaxation. Perform SQUID magnetometry (measuring M(H) loops in both parallel and perpendicular orientations and ZFC/FC M(T) curves) and derive −ΔSM(T) from temperature-dependent magnetization isotherms up to 50 kOe.
measurements: TEM/SAED and AFM to monitor structural changes
ZFC/FC M(T) curves and parallel/perpendicular M(H) loops via SQUID magnetometry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant enhancements in maximum magnetization and −ΔSM, or if there is no reduction in hysteresis compared to the as-deposited state—or if annealing leads to detectable bulk crystallization—then the hypothesis, which attributes improved magnetocaloric performance to strain relief and short-range reordering, must be rejected.
